- When sentiment is consistently negative (e.g., < -0.3) over recent days, model tends to overcorrect downward — adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid underestimating rebound.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >+5% from prior peak), model often overshoots and overpredicts continuation — reduce forecast peak by 5–10% to account for mean reversion.
- If model forecast is significantly below recent 18-day average (e.g., < 1.5σ below), and sentiment is neutral or slightly positive, increase forecast to align with mean reversion bias.
- When sentiment is positive (e.g., > 0.3) and model is overly conservative, add 2–3% to forecast to capture sentiment-driven momentum.
- For 30-day horizon, model often underestimates late-period volatility — increase final 5–7 days of forecast by 1–2% to reflect tail risk or sentiment-driven volatility clustering.
- If sentiment history shows repeated negative swings (e.g., alternating -0.3 to 0.0), model tends to lag — adjust forecast to be 1–2 days ahead of actual trend in such cycles.
